REPORT 
 No country is reported to be immune from the problem of adulterated or spurious drugs and India is 
no exception. While counterfeiting of consumer goods is a general problem, the issue of adulterated or 
spurious drugs acquires a much more serious dimensi on because it involves medicinal use. Spurious or 
adulterated drugs can cause serious, or even fatal injury, if they do not contain the required active 
ingredients or contain harmful substances. Reported large-scale production and trading of spurious drugs in 
India is a cause of concern not only to the consumers w ithin the country but is also  affecting the credibility 
of drug products from India. 
2. The Statement of Objects and Reasons appended to the Bill is as under:— 
 “The Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 is a consum er protection legislation, which is mainly 
concerned with the standards and quality of drugs manufactured in this country and control of the import, 
manufacture, sale and distribution of drugs and cosmet ics. There have been widespread reports regarding 
the easy movement and harmful consequences of adulterated and spurious drugs in the country and wide 
ranging national concern has been expressed on these re ports. The issue of adulterated or spurious drugs 
has serious dimensions because it in volves medicinal use and can lead to serious and even fatal injury. 
There is also loss of revenue to the Government due to the manufacture and sale of adulterated or spurious 
drugs. 
2.1 Drugs and Cosmetic Act, 1940 was amended in 1982 so as to impose more stringent penalties on the 
anti-social elements indulging in the manufacture or sa le of adulterated or spurious drugs or drugs not of 
standard quality which are likely to cause death or grievous hurt to  the user. However, the penalties 
existing in the said Act are not found effective. On e of the reasons for the existing penalties not being 
effective is that manufacture and sa le of adulterated and spurious drugs is primarily clandestine activity 
which is showing increasing involvement of organized crime in recent years. Besides, offenders often obtain 
bail as the offences are non-cognizable and bailabl e under the existing provisions of the Act. The 
offenders remain on bail due to delay in disposal of cases for manufacture and sale of adulterated and 
spurious drugs. Many cases for violation are detected and investigated by the police who needs to be 
conferred upon the power to prosecute such cases promptly. 
2.2 The Central Government cons tituted an Expert Committee under the chairmanship of Dr. R.A. 
Mashelkar, Director General of Council of Scientific and Industrial Research in January, 2003 to 
undertake a comprehensive examination of drugs regu latory issues, including the problem of spurious 
drugs, evaluate the extent of the problem of spurious or substandard drugs recommend measures required 
to deal with the problem effectively. The Committee, inter alia, recommended for enhancement of penalties, 
designation of Special Court for speedy trial of spurious  drugs cases, making offences relating to spurious 
drugs cognizable and non-bailable, authorising the poli ce to file prosecution for offences related to 
spurious drugs and compounding of offences, etc. A Bill to amend the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 
broadly to give effect to the reco mmendations of the aforesaid Committee was introduced on the 22nd 
December, 2003 in Lok Sabha and the Bill lapsed due to dissolution of Lok Sabha. 
3. Committee’s attention has been drawn by the very low rate of prosecution cases with regard to 
adulterated/spurious drugs and even lower rates of cases launched in the country. Following figures support 
the contention of the Committee:— 
Year Cases launched Cases decided 
2001-2002 538 171 
2002-2003 449 105 
2003-2004 570 166 
3.1 On a specific query about the factors responsib le for such a dismal scenario, the Committee was 
given to understand that different pattern of infrastruc ture and logistics for drugs quality control in States 
was primarily responsible. Prolonged procedure for settlement of court cases was another hindrance. The 

Committee notes that the Drugs and Cosmetics (Amendme nt) Bill, 2005 seeks to impose more stringent 
penalties on manufacture/sale of adulterated/spurio us/sub-standard drugs. The Committee, however, does 
not foresee any significant improvement, keeping in view  the existing manpower of 1040 Drug Inspectors 
and annual rate of 35,000 samples tested against total number of 11,000 Drug Manufacturers/Loan Licensee 
and 3,50,000 sales premises. The Committee observes that after passage of the Bill, the Government 
proposes to have interactive discussions with stat e authorities including police authorities and have 
orientation programmes arranged for its effective impl ementation. The Committee, however, is of the view 
that such initiatives alone will not serve the pu rpose. What is required is strengthening of 
infrastructure/manpower for drug quality control in all the States/UTs and its constant monitoring. 
4. The clauses in respect of which amendments ha ve been suggested by the Committee, are discussed 
in the succeeding paragraphs. 
Clause 2 
4.1 Clause 2 of the Bill proposes to amend Section 27 of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act-1940 regarding 
‘Penalty for manufacture, sale etc. of drugs’. As en umerated in the clause, penalties i.e. both term of 
imprisonment and amount of fine are proposed to be enhanced considerably for manufacture/ 
sale/distribution stocking/exhibiting/by any person di rectly or any other person on his behalf of 
adulterated/spurious/ not of standard quality drugs. The proposed amendment seeks to enhance the term of 
imprisonment which shall not be less than ten years but which may extend to imprisonment for life and also 
the amount of fine which shall not be less than ten lakh rupees or three times value of the drugs confiscated, 
whichever is more. 
4.2 The Committee has been given to understand that the proposed amendment is broadly based on the 
recommendations made by the Mashel kar Committee. The Committee, how ever, finds that there is a major 
difference. The Expert Committee’s recommendation for death penalty for the said offence has been 
replaced by imprisonment for life. The Committee wa s informed that this modification was made in 
pursuance of the directions from the Cabinet. All experts, representatives of associations and NGOs 
appearing before the Committee while welcoming  the increase in fine were also not in favour of death 
penalty. The Committee also holds the same view. 
4.3 While interacting with various stake-holders,  the Committee came across divergent views on the 
criteria for imposition of penalties. Apprehensions were  voiced about there being no difference in the level 
of penalty for different categories of persons. As a result, manufacturer/distributor/stockist/seller/person 
exhibiting or offering for sale/distribution or his nominee are liable to undergo the same penalty. Another 
viewpoint was that penalties should be commensurate with the gravity of offence. Penalties should be 
highest for such acts which are done deliberately with the clear intention of making profit. Punishment 
should be more severe in case of life-saving drugs. 
4.4 Response of the Ministry to these reservations was that the object of the Act is to deal strongly with 
the harmful consequences of spurious  drugs. It was a matter of national concern to safeguard the health of 
society from the harmful consequences and ill effects of  spurious drugs and hence, it becomes necessary to 
deal with the manufacturer and the dealer on the same footing with respect to spurious drugs in the larger 
interest of the society. The Committee is in agreement with the view point of the Ministry that the 
enhancement in penalty under Section 27 of the Act would act as a deterrent for offenders. 
4.5 Committee’s attention was also drawn to there being instances of patients suffering from prolonged 
illness primarily due to the use of spurious/adulterated drugs. However, such cases are not covered under 
section 27 (a). It was suggested that besides death an d grievous hurt, prolonged illness should also be made 
the criteria for imposition of fine/imprisonment. The Committee feels that prolonged illness might occur 
due to a variety of reasons. There may be ca ses where doctor inadvertently or deliberately  may be 
responsible for delay in getting the patient cured. However, if it is due to use of adulterated or 
spurious drugs, then this aspect needs to be l ooked into. The Committee, accordingly, recommends 
that the Department may explore the possibility of bringing such cases under Section 27 (a). 

4.6 Another suggestion made before the Committee was that ‘not of standard quality drugs’ should be 
taken out from the ambit of Section 27. It was emphas ized that ‘not of standard quality drugs’ should 
neither be confused with spurious or adulterated drug s nor construed as spurious or adulterated drugs. It 
was pointed out that quality parameters as were provid ed under Section 16 for such drugs cannot be treated 
at par with adulterated/spurious drugs and hence de serve comparatively lesser penalties. The Committee is, 
however, not inclined to agree with this view-point. The Committee notes that Section 16 and second 
schedule specifics the standard of quality to be maintained by drugs. In the case of patent or 
proprietary medicines, the list of ingredients is to be displayed in the prescribed manner on the label 
or container. In the case of vaccines, sera, toxins, toxoids, antitoxins, antigens and biological products 
of like nature, standards are to be maintained by the labs recognized by WHO from time to time. The 
Committee is of the view that any deviation in the prescribed standards of medicines is equally 
serious when compared wi th adulterated and spurious drugs an d needs to be treated at the same 
footing. 
4.7 Clause 2 (B) of the Bill seeks to insert two prov isos under Section 27 (a) whereby the victim or in 
the case of his death his relative is liable to be pa id the amount of fine as compensation. The Committee 
notes that by way of explanation an exhaustive list of ‘relatives’ has been given, which indicates that 
dependence on the deceased person’s earning is the sole criteria for making a relative eligible for 
compensation. The only exception is the spouse of the deceased person, minor legitimate son and 
unmarried legitimate daughter and a widowed mother. The Committee has strong reservations in this regard 
as in its opinion dependence on the deceased person should not be the only criteria as loss of loved one can 
never be compensated. It can be the criteria to increase the amount of compensation. 
4.8 A suggestion made to the Committee was that divorced /deserted sister or daughter-in law should also 
be covered under ‘relatives’. Rese rvation was also expressed about including only widowed mother. It was 
felt that mother needed to be include d. The Committee also observes that parents of infant child victim are 
not covered under the proposed definition. On a specific query in this regard, the Department has submitted 
“that the joint and harmonious reading of the second proviso and the Explanation (ii) of the term ‘relative’ 
makes it clear that a minor legitimate son/daughter as well as an infant, as the case may be, is a relative and 
hence covered under the said section”. The Committee is not convinced with the reply and feels that the 
Department, perhaps, has not addressed the issue appropriately. Apprehensions were also voiced 
about the chance of conflict in the event of there being more than one claimant being covered by the 
term ‘relative’. There was thus a need for categorizing the same. 
4.9 The Committee, accordingly, recommends that parents of infant victim should be covered 
under the definition of “relative” v ery explicitly so that the parents in  case of such an eventuality are 
not deprived of their right of compensation. 
4.10 Definition should also include deserted/divorced  sister/daughter-in law and mother instead of 
only widowed mother. The Committee is convinced by the clarification of the Department that it 
should be left to the co urt of law to decide the bona fide recipient and the quan tum of compensation 
to be paid to him/her. 
Clause 2 (ii), 3 and 4 
4.11 These clauses propose to enhance the penalty unde r Section 27 (b), (c) and (d), 28 and 28A of 
the Act. The Committee is in ag reement with these amendments a nd, accordingly, adopts these 
clauses. 
Clause-5 
5.1 Clause 5 seeks to increase the penalty for subseq uent offences by proposing amendments in clause 
(a) and (b) of Section 30. The Comm ittee, however, notes that clause (c) of Section 30 which deals with 
penalty for subsequent offences co mmitted under Section 27 (d) is propo sed to be deleted. Clause (c) 
provided that any person if again convicted of an offence under clause (d) of Section 27 shall be punishable 

with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less th en two years but which may extend to four years or 
with fine which shall not be less than five thousand rupees or with both. 
5.2 The Committee notes that Section 27 (d) provide s for penalty, i.e. imprisonment for a term which 
shall not be less then one year but which may extend to  two years and fine for sale/manufacture etc of any 
drug not covered by Clause (a), (b) and (c) of Section 27, in contravention of any provision under chapter 
IV of the Act or any rule making power thereunder. It  also gives the court discretionary powers to reduce 
the imprisonment term. The Committee fails to understand the ra tionale for deletion of this clause, 
especially whereas all other penalties under the ot her provisions under Chapter IV are proposed to 
be enhanced. Chapter IV deals with  manufacture, sale and distribution of drugs. Section-33 under 
this Chapter relates to the rules making power of the Central Government which include very vital 
subjects, for example, establishment of labs, methods of test/ analysis of drugs, qualification/duties of 
Govt. Analysts/ Inspectors, prohibition of sale/stocking/exhibition for sale/ distribution of drugs after 
the expiry date/specification of offence regarding wh ich order of confiscation is required to be made 
etc. As per Section 30 (c), penalty for subsequent  offence was more stringen t when compared with 
penalty for first offence under Section 27 (d). The Committee, therefore, is of the view that Section 30 
(c) should not be deleted and penalty for subsequent  offence in Section 30 (c) should be suitably 
enhanced. 
5.3 The Committee notes that Clause 5 also proposes deletion of Sub-Section (2) of Section 30. This 
Sub-Section relates to penalty for subsequent offence of use of Govt. Analysts report for advertising. 
Penalty for subsequent offence was higher then the pe nalty for the first offence i.e. against a fine for 
Rs. 500/- penalty for subsequent offence is maximum imprisonment of ten years or with fine or with 
both. No justification has been given by the Depa rtment for deletion of this Sub-section. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should review this amendment. 
Clause-6 
6.1 Clause 6 of the Bill proposes to substitute Sub-Section 1 and 2 of Section 32 relating to cognizance 
of offences. The Committee notes that this am endment is based on the Mashelkar Committee 
recommendations which suggested that in addition to the Drugs Inspectors, police authorities may also be 
authorized at an early stage to fi le prosecutions for spurious drugs offences. The Committee notes that a 
police officer not below the rank of Sub-Inspector has, accordingly, been given the power to prosecute in 
the Bill. The Committee, however, observes that pros ecution power is also proposed for Central/ State 
Govt. officers. On a specific query in this regard, th e Department submitted that due to there being a large 
number of vacancies of State Drug Inspectors remaining unfilled, it was th ought that to prevent delays and 
to expedite the process of prosecution, officers of the Central or State Government may also be authorized. 
6.2 One view which emerged before the Committee wa s that Drug Inspectors being conversant with 
drugs and its formulations, are most capable in assessi ng drug-related cases. Ap prehensions were voiced 
about involvement of police personnel which may lead to unnecessary harassment of the license holder. It 
was, accordingly, su ggested that involvement of police should only be made on written request from the 
Drugs Licensing Authority of the area. 
6.3 The Committee also feels that a police officer or an officer of the Central  Government or State 
Government do not have the requir ed professional qualification to  handle drug-related cases. 
Therefore, for the purpose of proper prosecution,  involvement of Drug Licensing Authority is 
necessary. The Committee, therefore, recommends that in case of pros ecution by the police inspector 
or Govt. Officer, prior permission of the Drug Li censing Authority of the concerned area should be 
made a precondition. 
Clause-7 
7. Clause 7 of the Bill proposes to insert a new section 32B after section 32 A which provides for 
compounding of offences. The Committee was given to understand that the power to compound the offence 

should not be made so simple or easy that it is le ft entirely to the discretion of the Govt. officer. The 
procedure should be made more transparent. To ac hieve these objectives ther e should be certain pre-
requisites for compounding. Firstly, the aggrieved party’s concurrence should be there. Secondly, the 
amount compounded should be adequate to compensate the aggrieved person. Thirdly, the cost of litigation 
should also be included in the sum compounded. The Committee concurs with this view and 
recommends the Department to amend Section 32 B in the light of the above observation. 
Clause-10 
8.1 Clause 10 of the Bill proposes to insert a new Section 36 AB which mentions about designating one 
or more Courts of Sessions as special court for the trial of such offences. 
8.2 The Committee would like to mention that th e Expert Committee had recommended constitution of 
Special Courts and not the designation of some selected Courts as Special Courts for speedy trial of drug 
related offences. On a specific query, the Department  has submitted that setting up of Special Courts by 
designating existing courts would save time. However, if new courts have to be set up as Special Courts, 
then this issue would have to be resolved in consultation with Ministry of Law. The Committee, however, 
is not inclined to believe that mere designation of one or more courts of Sessions as Special Court will 
help in expeditious disposal of cases as the Sessi ons Courts are already ov erburdened with a large 
number of cases. The Committee, therefore, recomme nds that new courts need to be set up for the 
purpose of trying offences under the Drugs & Cosmetics Act. 
9. The Committee adopts the remaining clauses of  the Bill, including enacting formula and the 
title without any amendment. 
General 
10. The Committee has taken note of the suggestion of the Expert Commi ttee that a specific provision, 
on the lines of the Narcotics Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act-1985, needs to be made in the Drugs 
and Cosmetics Act-1940 that will allow the person indulging in the spurious drug offences to be detained 
for a minimum period of three months. This would serv e as an effective deterrent for such offenders. 
Explaining the reasons for not including this recommendation of the Committee, the Ministry submitted 
that the proposed Act envisages imprisonment for a term which shall be not less than ten years but which 
may extend to imprisonment for life and shall also be liable to fine which shall not be less than ten lakh 
rupees or three times the value of the drugs confiscated, whichever is more, to all those persons indulging in 
offences pertaining to spurious drugs. The Comm ittee has also been given to understand that these 
provisions will work as an effective deterrent and are far more stringent than NDPS Act. The Committee 
would, however, like to point out that intera ction with various stake-holder s indicates that persons accused 
of manufacturing or trading in spurious or adulterated drugs usually get bail very easily and thereafter either 
intimidate or influence the witnesses and try to win ov er them. They also manipulate the administrative and 
judicial system. In this manner they  weaken the case of the prosecuti on and such cases thus drag on for 
years together. The conviction rate, due to the reason s mentioned above, is very low in drug related 
offences. The Committee, therefore, thinks  that in order to realize the deterrent effects of the 
proposed Bill, first of all a successful conviction in the court of law is necessary and for that to 
happen it should be ensured that the accused is prevented from manipulating the system to his 
advantage. The Committee also feels that peddling in spurious or adulterated drugs is no way less 
serious than peddling in narcotics. The Committ ee, therefore, recommends that the Department 
should incorporate similar provisions in the Bill, as exist in the NDPS Act. 
11. The Committee is constrained to observe that ther e is no mechanism to make aware the consumers or 
public at large about the harmful effect of certain drugs or banned drugs. The Committee 
strongly feels that the Central Govt. needs to make efforts for publishing a list of banned drugs for the 
information of all concerned. The Committee was inform ed that a New Task Force on the subject is being 
set up which will review the existing procedure for dr ug verification to make it more user friendly. The 

Committee emphasizes that action to increase public awareness abou t harmful/banned drugs should 
be initiated at the earliest.  
12. It is a well-known fact that a drug manufacturer in one state mo ves freely in interstate commerce as 
well as in export market. However, the infrastru cture facilities, the number and quality of drug 
inspectors, testing facilities support systems etc. cont inue to vary significantly from State to State. Not 
only this, a large number of States still do not have  drug-testing labs. The Committee finds that out of 
the 17 drugs testing labs functioning in different States , only 7 are reported to have the capacity to test 
all categories of drugs. In view of  such a situation, there is an urgent need for not only establishing 
viable testing facilities but also providing Intelligence Cells working in coordination with the different 
States. The Committee has been informed that un der the World Bank assisted Capacity Building 
project for Food Safety and Quality Control of Drugs, upgradation/construction of at least one state of 
the art Drug Testing Laboratory in each State/UT a nd also some central labs is already in progress. 
Besides, in order to introduce further uniformity in the implementation of the Drugs and Cosmetices 
Act in the States, selected labs in the States are being provided with modern equipment and trainings 
are being provided to both the laboratory and drug re gulatory personnel. Simila rly, an IEC strategy is 
being developed for ensuring a bette r-informed and more aware consumer. The Committee hopes that 
with all these measures the situation would improve in the States. 
 Committee’s attention has been drawn by another observation made by the Mashelkar Committee for 
there being a need for surveillance over distribution of drugs through medical practitioners. The 
Department also accepts this observa tion as distribution of drugs throu gh medical practitioners is a major 
channel of distribution of spurious/adulterated dr ugs. Medical practitioners are exempted from the 
provisions of the Chapter IV of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act dealing with manufacture, sale and 
distribution of drugs and Rules made there under (Entry 5 of Schedule ‘K’ of the Rules). The Committee 
has, however, been given to underst and that many registered medica l practitioners dispensing drugs to 
their patients, do not always purchase their supplies from authorized sources. On a specific query about 
putting a check on such activities, the Committee was informed that provisions are already in existence to 
inspect the stock of drugs retained by the Register ed Medical Practitioners and procurement of drugs in 
such cases should be made from authorized dealer wi th proper purchase voucher. In case of spurious 
drugs, the concerned Medical Practitioner should also be made an accused if the investigation so reveal. 
However, when asked about number of such cases of violation by medical practitioners registered so far, 
the Drug Controller General of India categorically admitted that not even a single case has been registered 
so far. The Committee finds it rather surprising. The Committee strongly feels that the Department has to 
take in the initiative in this matter. An effective monitoring mechanism needs to be set up to present such 
cases. At the same time, public should also be made aware of such provisions. 
 The Committee observes that the definition of  adulterated and spurious drugs - Allopathic, 
Ayurvedic, Unani and Siddha drugs is the same. Howe ver, similar provision for penalty for manufacture, 
sale etc. of AYUSH drugs is not there. As per media reports, Ayurvedic drugs containing metals and 
steroids are in circulation and sometimes cause griev ous hurt to the users. On a specific query in this 
regard, Department clarified that presence of metals and steroids in Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani 
medicines could be due to the contamination of raw material of natural origin i.e. soil-water 
contamination. Therefore, raw material testing to exclude the heavy metal presence above the permissible 
level is needed which requires good laboratories to undertake this testing at an affordable time. This will 
add to the cost of AYUSH medicine significantly. Ph ytosteroids are also present in plants naturally. 
Therefore, only adulteration of steroid should be penal offence. The Committee observes that Section 33(1) 
and (J) of the Drugs & Cosmetics Act provides pena lty for manufacture, sale etc. of spurious and 
adulterated Ayurvedic, Siddha drugs and for subsequent offences respectively. The Committee however 
feels that more stringent penalties are required to be  imposed in the case of spurious/adulterated/not of 
standard quality Ayurvedic/Unani/Sidd ha drugs also. The Committee, ther efore, is of the view that the 
penalty provision for AYUSH drug should be reviewed so as to make changes, if necessary. The 

Committee also emphasizes the need for strengthenin g the testing labs for AYUSH drugs, the present 
status of which cannot be considered satisfactory.

 The Committee hopes that with all these measur es the situation would improve in the States. 
   (Para 12) 
 The Committee finds it rather surprising. The Committee strongly feels that the Department has to 
take in the initiative in this matter. An effective monitoring mechanism needs to be set up to present such 
cases. At the same time, public should also be made aware of such provisions. (Para 13(ii)) 
 The Committee however feels that mo re stringent penalties are required to be imposed in the case 
of spurious/adulterated/ not of standard qualit y Ayurvedic/Unani/Siddha dr ugs also. The Committee, 
therefore, is of the view that the penalty provision for AYUSH drug should be reviewed so as to make 
changes, if necessary. The Committee also emphasizes  the need for strengthening the testing labs for 
AYUSH drugs, the present status of which cannot be considered satisfactory. (Para 14)

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 
The Drugs and Cosmetics Act. 1940 is a consumer protection legislation, 
which is mainly concerned with the standards and quality of drugs manufactured in 
this country and control of the import, manufacture, sale and distribution of drugs 
and cosmetics. 
2. There have been widespread reports regarding the easy movement and 
harmful consequences of adulterated and spurious drugs in the country and wide 
ranging national concern has been expressed on these reports. The issue of 
adulterated or spurious drugs has serious dimensions because it involves medicinal 
use and can lead to serious and even fatal in jury. There is also loss of revenue to the 
Government due to the manufacture and sale of adulterated or spurious drugs. 
3. Drugs and Cosmetic Act, 1940 was amended in 1982 so as to impose more 
stringent penalties on the anti-social elements indulging in the manufacture or sale of 
adulterated or spurious drugs or drugs no t of standard qualiry which are likely to 
cause death or grievous hurt to the user. Ho wever, the penalties existing in the said 
Act are not found effective. One of the r easons for the existing penalties not being 
effective is that manufacture and sale of adulterated and spurious drugs is primarily 
clandestine activity which is showing incr easing involvement of organised crime in 
recent years. Besides, offenders often obtain  bail as the offences are non-cognizable 
and bailable under the existing provisions of the Act. The offenders remain on bail 
due to delay in disposal of cases for manufacture and sale of adulterated and spurious 
drugs. Many cases for violation are detected and investigated by the police who 
needs to be conferred upon the power to prosecute such cases promptly. 
4. The Central Government constitu ted an Expert Committee under the 
chairmanship of Dr. R.A. Mashelkar, Director General of Council of Scientific and 
Industrial Research in January, 2003 to undertake a comprehensive examination of 
drugs regulatory issues, including the problem of spurious drugs, evaluate the extent 
of the problem of spurious or sub-standard drugs and recommend measures required 
to deal with the problem effectively. The Committee, inter alia, recommended for 
enhancement of penalties, designation of Special Court for speedy trial of spurious 
drugs cases, making offences relating to spurious drugs and cognizable and non-
bailable, authorising the police to file pros ecution for offences related to spurious 
drugs and compounding of offences, etc. A Bill to amend the Drugs and Cosmetics 
Act, 1940 broadly to give effect to the recommendations of the aforesaid Committee 
was introduced on the 22nd December, 2003 in Lok Sabha and the Bill lapsed due to 
dissolution of Lok Sabha. The Central Government, inter alia, proposes to make the 
following amendments in the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, broadly on the lines of 
the earlier Bill introduced with certain modifications which relate to enhancement of 
punishment and doing away with the death penalty as proposed in the said Bill, 
namely:— 
(i) The existing provisions contained in  section 27 of the aforesaid Act, inter 
alia, provide for scale of punishment for the firs t offence in respect of adulterated or 
spurious drugs. Clause (a) of section 27 of the aforesaid Act, provides for imprison-
ment for not less than five years which may extend to life and with fine of not less 
than rupee:; ten thousand for the manufacture and sale of adulterated or spurious 
drugs or drugs not of standard quality which are likely to cause death of the patients 
or harm on the patient’s body as would amount  to grievous hurt. It is proposed to 
enhance the period of imprisonment fur a term which shall not be less than ten years 

but which may externd to imprisonment for life and shall also be liable 10 fine of ten 
lakh rupees or three times the value of the drugs confiscated, whichever is more: 
(ii) It is also proposed to insert two provisos in the said clause (a) so as to 
provide that the fine imposed on the convicted person and realised from him under 
the said clause shall be paid to the person who used such adulterated or spurious drug 
and in case of his death, to his relative: 
(iii) Clause (b) of said section 27 provides for punishment of imprisonment for 
not less than one year which may extend to three years and fine of not less than 
rupees five thousand for manufacture and sale of any adulterated drug (not being a 
drug referred to in section 17A) or manufacture and sale of drugs without a valid 
licence. It is proposed to enhance the said punishment of imprisonment being not less 
than three years but may extend to five y ears and with fine which shall not be less 
than one lakh rupees; 
(iv) Clause (c) of aforesaid section 27 provides for punishment of 
imprisonment for not less than one year wh ich may extend to three years but which 
may extend to five years and with fine wh ich shall not be less than rupees five 
thousand for manufacture and sale of any spurious drug (not being a drug referred to 
in section 17B). It is proposed to enhance the said punishment of imprisonment being 
not less than seven years but which may extend to imprisonment for life and with 
fine which shall be three lakh rupees or three times the value of the drugs seized, 
whichever is more; 
(v) Clause (d) of aforesaid section 27 provides for punishment of 
imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than one year but which may extend 
to two years and with fine. It is proposed to provide that the fine shall not be less 
than twenty thousand rupees; 
(vi) It is also proposed to provide for a fine of not less than twenty thousand 
rupees under section 28 for non-disclosure of the name of the manufacturer and 
under section 28 A for not keeping docum ents, etc., and for not disclosure of 
information; 
(vii) It is also proposed to enhance punishment specified under section 30 for 
subsequent offences. Clause (a) of said section 30 provides for punishment for 
imprisonment not less than rwo years which may extend to six years and with fine of 
not less than rupees ten thousand for manufacture and sale of any adulterated drug or 
manufacture and sale of drugs without a valid licence. It is proposed to enhance the 
said punishment which shall not be less th an seven years but which may extend to 
ten years and with fine which shall not be less than rwo lakh rupees. Clause (b) of 
aforesaid section 30 provides for punishment for imprisonment for not less than six 
years which may extend to ten years and with fine o’f not less than rupees ten 
thousand for manufacture and sale ofa spuri ous drug. It is proposed to enhance the 
punishment of imprisonment which shall not be less than ten years but which may 
extend to imprisonment for life and with fine which shall not be less than three lakh 
rupees; 
(viii) It is also proposed to designate one or more Court of Session as Special 
Court for trial of offences related to adulterated or spurious drugs; 
(ix) It is also proposed to make offences relating to adulterated or spurious ‘ 
drugs as cognizable and non-bailable in certain cases; 

(x) It is also proposed to confer power s upon the police officers not below the 
rank of sub-inspector of police and other officers of the Central Government or State 
Government authorised by it to institute the prosecution under the aforesaid Act; 
(xi) It is also proposed to provide compounding of certain offences not being 
an offence punishable with imprisonment only or with imprisonment and also with 
fine. 
5.   The Bill seeks to achieve the above objects

MEMORANDUM REGARDING DELEGATED LEGISLATION 
Clause 7 of the Bill proposes to insert a new section 32B in the Drugs and 
Cosmetics Act, 1940 to provide for compounding of certain offences by the Central 
Government or. by any State Government or any officer authorised in this behalf by the 
Central Government or a State Government on payment for credit to that government of 
such sum as that Government may, by rules specify. Clause 8 of the Bill proposes to 
insert a clause (r) in sub-section (2) of section 33 of the said Act to confer power upon 
the Central Government to make such rules. 
2. The matter in respect of which rules may be made are matter of procedure and 
detail and it is not practicable to provide for it in the Bill itself. The delegation of 
legislative power is, therefore, of a normal character.

I. INTRODUCTION 
1.1 The Ministry of AYUSH has the mandate to develop AYUSH systems viz Ayurveda, 
Yoga & Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Sowa -Rigpa and Homeopathy. In keeping with the 
policy of the Government to lay focused thrust on the India Traditional Systems of Medicine, 
the Department of AYUSH was granted status of M inistry w.e.f. 9 th November, 2014.  The 
Ministry is working with a vision to position AYUSH systems as the preferred systems of 
living and practice for attaining a healthy India. 
1.2 The Ministry has identified its mission in terms of seven board thematic areas of 
AYUSH activities.  The thematic areas are as follows:- 
(i) Effective Human Resource Development 
(ii) Provision of Quality AYUSH Services 
(iii) Information, Education and Communication 
(iv) Quality Research in AYUSH 
(v) Growth of the Medical Plants Sector 
(vi) Drug Administration 
(vii) International Exchange Programme/Seminars/Workshops on AYUSH

II BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
 2.1 The projected demand of funds of the Ministry of AYUSH was to the tune of Rs. 
5035.27 crores for 2020 -21.  However, the Ministry has been allocated only Rs. 2122.08 
crores thus leaving a shortfall of Rs. 2913.19 crores.  Similar situation prevailed last year also 
as is evident from the table below:-

2.2 The Secretary in his deposition before the Committee highlighted the fact that the 
projected requirement of the Ministry was realistic as the Ministry needed the allocation to 
tide over funds constraints.  The major areas that will be affected due to less allocation of 
funds for the year 2020-21as informed by the Ministry are as follows: 
 
(i) National AYUSH Mission (NAM) - NAM is the only Centrally Sponsored flagship 
programme of this Ministry under National Health Mission.  An amount of 
Rs.1000.00 crore was projected against which an allocation of Rs.540.00 is provided 
leaving a shortfall of Rs.460.00 crore.   
(ii) Health and We llness Centres- This Scheme is a part of Ayushman Bharat project 
being implemented through National AYUSH Mission of this Ministry. It is proposed 
to establish 12500 AYUSH Centres across the country.  Though an amount of 
Rs.150.00 crore was made available for the scheme during the year 2019-20, no funds 
could be utilized due to non approval of the Scheme. An amount of Rs.971.34 crore 
was projected for the year 2020 -21 but an amount of Rs.165.00 crores could only be 
provided within the overall resources allo cated to this Ministry leaving a shortfall of 
Rs.806.34 crore.   
(iii) Champion Sector Scheme - This is a new Scheme being implemented under the 
nodal Ministry of Commerce.  The Ministry of AYUSH is also one of the 
implementing Ministries.  Though an amount of Rs .50.00 crore was allocated during 
the year 2019-20, the same could not be utilized due to non -approval of the Scheme. 
An amount of Rs.221.17 crore was projected for the year 2020 -21 but only Rs.21.20 
crore could be provided within the overall resources pro vided to the Ministry leading 
to a shortfall of Rs.199.97 crore. 
(iv) Autonomous Bodies 
 
(a) Construction Projects- This Ministry ha d projected an amount of Rs.673.58 crore 
under GIA Capital for the completion of ongoing construction projects being 
undertaken in various National Institutes and Research Councils, out of which an 
amount of Rs.411.54 crore could only be allocated within th e available allocation of 
this Ministry. To overcome the shortage to some extent, this Ministry had separately 
sought a loan of Rs.1000/ - crore from Higher Education Funding Agency (HEFA) to 
support, in particular, the 8 construction projects of National I nstitutes.  The total 
project cost of these 8 construction projects is Rs.1628.76crore, out of which, an 

3 
 
amount of Rs.281.65 crore has already been spent out of the allocation of this 
Ministry so far.   EFC proposals for taking loan have already been submi tted to the 
Ministry of Finance and the approval is still awaited.  In case, the said amount is 
approved through HEFA as a loan, the shortfall indicated above would be reduced to 
that extent 
(b) GIA – General-In the 17 Autonomous Bodies of this Ministry , the funds allocated 
under GIA -General is utilized for Research, payment of stipends, scholarships, 
medicines, salaries of outsourced staff etc. apart from incurring day to day 
expenditures.  
Under GIA General against a projected demand of Rs.673.58 crore for 2020-21, the 
actual allocation possible within the total resources allocated to this Ministry was 
Rs.411.51 crore leading to a shortfall of Rs.262.07 crore. 
2.3 The Ministry submitted that it has made continuous and persistent efforts for adequate 
budgetary support. The efforts started during the pre -budget discussions with the Ministry of 
Finance held on 08.11.20219 followed by a meeting of Secretary (AYUSH) with Secretary 
(Expenditure) on 02.01.2020 and 30.01.2020. The Secretary (AYUSH) again took up the 
matter with the Secretary (Economic Affairs) through D.O. letter dated 02.01.2020 and even 
by personally meeting him again. Hon‘ble  MoS (IC), Ministry of AYUSH also held a 
meeting with the Finance Minister on 09.01.2020 to apprise  the situation and requested to 
enhance the allocation under RE 2019 -20 as well as BE 2020 -21.  Due to these efforts the 
Ministry of Finance increased the RE allocation from Rs.1756.83 crore to Rs.1857.00 crore.  
However, no additional funds have been provided in BE 2020-21. 
2.4 The Committee is disappointed to note that against the projected demand of Rs. 
5035.27 crore for 2020-21, the Ministry of AYUSH has been allocated Rs. 2122.08 crores 
reflecting huge shortfall of Rs. 2913.19 crores.  The budgetary es timates of 2020 -21 
when compared with RE 2019 -20 indicate a marginal increase of Rs. 265.08 crores only 
for the Ministry. The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Ministry to get 
enhanced allocation but could not succeed . The Committee is constrai ned to note that 
several schemes of the Ministry would be affected due to shortfall of funds. The 
Committee apprehends that the objectives of important schemes like National Ayush 
Mission, Health and Wellness centres etc would not be fulfilled  due to financial 
constraints. Moreover, several research projects, construction work of National 
Institutes and Research Councils would also get affected.  The Committee takes note of 
submission of the Ministry to make up the shortfall of funds by seeking a loan of 
Rs.1000 crore from Higher Education Funding Agency (HEFA) , to support, in 
particular, the 8 construction projects of National Institutes.  The Committee is 
surprised to note that financial constraints have forced the Ministry to raise loan which 
shows that Government is not very serious towards promoting AYUSH and letting it 
emerge as an alternative and economical system of medicine . The Committee, however, 
is of the view that that the Ministry, being a relatively new one requires adequate funds  
and resources  for proving its efficacy and worth . The Committee, in its previous 
Reports, has consistently been emphasizing upon substantial increase in the allocation 

4 
 
to the Ministry for  executing its various schemes/programmes . The Committee, 
therefore, strongly, recommends the Ministry to  approach Ministry of Finance at RE  
stage with the request for additional demand so that implementation of schemes of the 
Ministry are not affected , adversely. It also recommends to the Ministry to  utilize the 
allocated funds optimally  with focus on the priority areas and make best use of the 
available funds. 
2.5 The Committee notes a difference of Rs. 1693.3 crore in the projected demand of 
Rs. 4469.59 crore in BE 2019 -20 and the demand of Rs. 2776.29 crore at the RE stage.  
This, according to the Committee, speaks volumes not only about the paradigms shift in 
its original conceived schemes but also utilization capacity of the Ministry.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry must make realistic assessment of 
its fund requirement  keeping in view on -going projects/projects to be undertaken  and 
accordingly project its demand.

management strategies and policy interventions could be suitably modified in view of 
any changes in the demand pattern.

medicinal plant species in high volume trade. 
 Immediate assessment of the status of wild population of medicinal plant species in 
high consumption which are also of high conservation concern and appropriate 
management interventions for building up populations of such species be worked out. 
 A system of backward linkage of the raw material consumed by the herbal 
manufacturing units to their source of production be developed and put in place. 
 The existing system of coding of botanicals in foreign  trade be critically evaluated and 
improved to establish clear linkage of traded materials with their plant source. 
 Support studies for reviewing the plant identities in respect of raw dongs obtained from 
more than one/ controversial plant source.

cultivation so as to accord focus to conservation of species which are in short supply.

3.13 The Committee would also like to emphasize that India is known to be a treasure

5.4 To a  query about the progress made as a result of the Pharmacovigilance Initiative for

pharmacovigilance initiative for ASU&H drugs since implementation of the Central Scheme 
in December, 2019 , three –tier network of pharmacovigilance centres has been established 
comprising of a National Pharmacovigilance Coordination Centre ( All India Institute of 
Ayurveda, New De lhi), five Intermediary Pharmacovigilance Centres (National Institutes of  
ASU&H) and 62  Peripheral Pharmacovigilance Centres (27 of Ayurveda, 14 of Siddha, 10 
of Unani and 11 of Homoeopathy)  across the country.  Since January 2019, the three -tier 
pharmacovigilance network has taken up the task of reporting adverse drug events and doing 
surveillance of misleading advertisements of ASU&H appearing in print and TV media for 
reporting to State regulatory authorities.  More than 4800 cases of misleading adver tisements 
were reported from August 2018 to December, 2019 and 324 Adverse Events of ASU&H 
were reported during the period from January 2019 to December, 2019.  Steering & 
Monitoring Committee, Technical Advisory Committee and Central Signal Detection & 
Causality Assessment Committee have been set up to implement the pharmacovigilance 
initiative effectively and analyse the Adverse Drug Reactions (ADRs) of ASU&H drugs  
consumed by the people for regulatory actions.  A website www.ayushsuraksha.com  has also

online submission of suspected ADR reports in a standard format.  Awareness building 
programs, CMEs, Training Programs, Na tional Conference and Workshops have been 
conducted to develop the culture of reporting adverse effects emanating from the use of 
ASU&H drugs and monitoring of advertisements having inappropriate contents and 
exaggerated claims.  IEC materials have been designed and disseminated for awareness of the 
public and stakeholders.

misleading advertisements. With the Steering & Monitoring Committee, Technical

(v) Support herbal industry and export market driven cultivation of medicinal pl ants 
with backward & forward linkages of marketing, post -harvest management and 
certification  
(vi) Integration of medicinal plants in farming systems and 
(vii) Increase export of value added items of medicinal plants.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS- AT A GLANCE 
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
 The Committee is disappointed to note that against the projected demand of Rs. 
5035.27 crore for 2020-21, the Ministry of AYUSH has been allocated Rs. 2122.08 crores 
reflecting huge shortfall of Rs. 2913.19 crores.  The budgetary estimates of 2020 -21 
when compared with RE 2019-20 indicate a marginal increase of Rs. 265.08 crores only 
for the Ministry. The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Ministry to get 
enhanced allocation but could not succeed. The Committee is constrained to note that 
several schemes of the Ministry would be affected due to shortfall of funds. The 
Committee apprehends that the objectives of important schemes like National Ayush 
Mission, Health and Wellness centres etc would not be fulfilled due to financial 
constraints. Moreov er, several research projects, construction work of National 
Institutes and Research Councils would also get affected.  The Committee takes note of 
submission of the Ministry to make up the shortfall of funds by seeking a loan of 
Rs.1000 crore from Higher Education Funding Agency (HEFA), to support, in 
particular, the 8 construction projects of National Institutes. The Committee is 
surprised to note that financial constraints have forced the Ministry to raise loan which 
shows that Government is not very ser ious towards promoting AYUSH and letting it 
emerge as an alternative and economical system of medicine. The Committee, however, 
is of the view that that the Ministry, being a relatively new one requires adequate funds 
and resources for proving its efficacy  and worth.  The Committee, in its previous 
Reports, has consistently been emphasizing upon substantial increase in the allocation 
to the Ministry for executing its various schemes/programmes . The Committee, 
therefore, strongly, recommends the Ministry to approach Ministry of Finance at RE 
stage with the request for additional demand so that implementation of schemes of the 
Ministry are not affected, adversely. It also recommends to the Minist ry to utilize the 
allocated funds optimally  with focus on the priority areas and make best use of the 
available funds. 
(Para 2.4) 
 The Committee notes a difference of Rs. 1693.3 crore the projected demand of 
Rs. 4469.59 crore in BE 2019 -20 and the demand o f Rs. 2776.29 crore at the RE stage 
highlighting.  This, according to the Committee, speaks volumes not only about the 
paradigms shift in its original conceived schemes but also utilization capacity of the 
Ministry.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry must make realistic 
assessment of its fund requirement keeping in view on -going projects/projects to be 
undertaken and accordingly project its demand. 
(Para 2.5) 
 The Committee is constrained to observe that the amount of allocation for the  
Ministry of AYUSH is very low as compared to the allocation made to Ministry of 
Health. The Committee is of the view that in order to explore the full potential of Ayush 
systems, it is imperative to allocate sufficient funds. The Committee in its 108 th Report 
had recommended that atleast 5% of the total Health Budget should be earmarked for 
AYUSH Ministry. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation of 
earmarking atleast 5% of the total Health Budget for the Ministry. 
(Para 2.8) 
 The Committee finds that the trend of utilization of budgetary allocation of the 
Ministry has been quite satisfactory till the fiscal year 2017 -18 but thereafter the 

27 
 
Ministry has not been able to make optimum utilization of allocated fund.  However, the 
Committee is anguished to find that the Ministry would receive 15.51% of the RE as 
late as in March, 2020 thereby leaving a very short span of time to spend on the on -
going project/schemes. The Committee, therefore, urges upon the Ministry to ensure 
full utilization the allocated funds so that its demand for additional funds is justified at 
RE stage or from next financial year. 
(Para 2.14) 
 The Committee observes that the reasons for under -utilization of allocated funds 
are mainly administrative which could ha ve easily been avoided had there been proper 
prudential monitoring and supervision during execution of the on -going 
projects/schemes.  The Committee is of the firm view that proper co -ordination and 
financial controlling needs to be spearheaded on all the construction activities 
undertaken so that funds are not left idle due to delays in construction causing time as 
well as cost overruns. Similarly, filing up of vacant posts in all the institutes/bodies 
under the Ministry should be accorded priority.  Also,  delay or non-receipt of adequate 
proposals from stakeholders especially States/UTs for any scheme indicates that the 
scheme needs to be restructured and incentivized to attract viable proposals for various 
schemes. The Committee would recommend the Minist ry to be vigilant and monitor the 
progress of on -going activities for all the schemes so that the physical as well financial 
targets of various schemes as set in Output-Outcome Statement are accomplished.   
(Para 2.16) 
 The Committee takes cognizance of th e measures taken by the Ministry for 
liquidation of UCs and do not find them to be very effective in tackling this problem. 
The number of pending UCs has mounted to 1222 amounting to Rs. 1093.45 crores till 
31.01.2020. The Committee, however, is also const rained to note that the dedicated 
portal for facilitating online transmission of UCs is still not operational. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the dedicated portal for online submission of 
UCs be made operational at the earliest and in any case d uring 2020 -21 so that the 
problem of pendency of UCs is tackled efficaciously and procedure is made more 
transparent and easy to monitor as well.  
(Para 2.19) 
 The Committee observes that maximum number of UCs are pending under 
National AYUSH Mission follo wed by National Medicinal Plants Board. As on 
31.02.2020, 468 UCs of NMPB amounting to Rs. 113.41 crores and 592 UCs of NAM 
amounting to Rs. 941.98 crores are pending. The Committee is anguished to observe the 
status of the Pendency of UCs in many States u nder NAM States/UTs like Assam, 
Jharkhand, Maharashtra, Meghalaya, Odisha, Chandigarh, Dadar & Nagar Haveli and 
Daman & Diu did not even liquidate a single UC in the years 2018-19 and 2019-20. 
(Para 2.23) 
 The Committee is of the firm view that the Ministr y needs to make concerted 
efforts for liquidation of pending UCs. Taking into account mounting number of 
pending UCs and the thousand of crores of fund blocked,  the Committee strongly 
recommends setting up of a monitoring cell to monitor the pendency of UC s and co -
ordinate and liaise with the defaulting States/UTs aggressively.   
(Para 2.24) 
 

28 
 
NATIONAL MEDICAL PLANTS BOARD 
 The Committee is constrained to note that high pendency of UCs is one of the 
problems affecting NMPB also and hence the Ministry needs to take necessary measures 
to deal with it.  This can be done by constant monitoring and persistent persuasion of 
the implementing agencies/States.  This is all the more necessary because pendency of 
UCs lead to blockage of release of funds and affects accomplishment of set objectives.  
(Para 3.5) 
 The Committee is of the view that given the mandate of NMPB, it requires to 
have adequate manpower to effectively carry out its functions.  The Committee wonders 
about the proposal for creation of 65 new posts for the Board which is still awaiting the 
light of the day. The Committee feels that human resource planning is being total ly 
ignored by the Ministry at the cost of functioning of the Board. The Committee is of the 
view that given the pivotal role NMPB plays in matters relating to medicinal plants in 
the country, the Ministry needs to augment human resources for NMPB to ensure  its 
smooth functioning.   
(Para 3.7) 
 The Committee takes note of the increasing volume of export of medicinal plants 
but is not satisfied with the pace of its growth.  The Committee feels that India is rich in 
unique and expensive  medicinal plants having vast potential export of such plants, but 
appropriate focus and priority needs to be given.  
(Para 3.9) 
 The Committee hopes that its recommendations to strengthen the whole sector of 
medicinal plants will receive due consideration . The Committee appreciates the 
initiatives being taken by the NMPB, however, much more needs to be done.  The 
Committee recommends for rationalizing schemes for promotion of commercial 
cultivation so as to accord focus to conservation of species which are in short supply .  
The support of the State Medicinal Plants Boards is desirable for better conservation 
and utilization of the national resources. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
NMPB to co-ordinate with SMPBs. 
(Para 3.12) 
   The Committee would also like to emphasize that India is known to be a treasure 
trove of medicinal plants. What is required is to identify, conserve and gratefully use 
them for medicinal purposes. Therefore, focus of the Board should be on utilizing the 
rich biodiversity on a sustainable basis.  The Committee would also like to highlight the 
pivotal role that the local community can play in development, conservation and 
sustainable use of such plants. The Committee, in this regard, recommends the NMPB 
to popularize a programme for sustainable dev elopment of Medicinal Plants amongst 
the local community.  
(Para 3.13) 
QUALITY CONTROL OF AYURVEDA, SIDDHA, UNANI AND HOMEOPATHIC 
(AYUSH) DRUGS 
 The Committee time and again has been emphasizing upon a stringent 
regulatory framework for quality control of ASU&H drugs.  The Committee believes 
that for AYUSH systems to emerge as a strong alternative system of medicine, it is 
imperative that its credibility is enhanced through proper monitoring, quality control of 
drugs by scientific validation, proper parameters for clinical trials, upgradation of drug 

29 
 
testing labs, GMP compliance by manufacturing units, control of misleading 
advertisements, etc. The Committee taking note of all the achievements would like to 
recommend   that quality control of ASU&H drugs is one of the most important areas 
within the AYUSH ambit which needs to be accorded utmost priority.  There is also a 
need for integration of AYUSH system of medicine with the modern system which is 
only possible through scientific validation and strict qual ity control for safety and 
efficacy of this system of medicine. The Committee strongly recommends for expediting  
and bringing forth the legislation for a regulatory umbrella for the education and 
profession of Pharmacy in Indian Medicine and Homoeopathy. 
(Para 4.4) 
The Committee is disappointed to note that regulatory posts for Central AYUSH 
vertical structure has yet not been finalized as the approval of the UPSC is awaited and 
the regular incumbents have yet not been appointed. Temporary arrangements hav e 
been made with the Technical Officers of the Ministry taking charge of the new role. 
The Committee believes that without the requisite manpower, the said structure would 
not be able to carry out its mandate. The Committee therefore recommends that the 
vertical structure of AYUSH within CDCSO should be made functional without further 
delay with all the incumbents in place. The Committee is also of the view that given the 
important role of this structure, enhanced funds  is the need of the hour to effective ly 
accomplish the envisaged objectives under the scheme. 
(Para 4.8) 
PHARMACOVIGILANCE INITIATIVES FOR ASU DRUGS 
 The Committee observes that a very low amount of allocation is being made for 
the scheme bearing a very vital mandate.  Even though the utiliza tion of this paltry 
allocation is not quite  satisfactory, the Committee is of the view that adequate and an 
enhanced allocation for this scheme is essential to create a strong Pharmacovigilance 
network across the country so as to ensure effective control of misleading 
advertisements, safety monitoring of ASU&H drugs, documentations and analysis of 
Adverse Drug Reactions, etc. The Committee, therefore, recommends sufficient 
enhancement of funds for the scheme at RE stage.  
(Para 5.3) 
 The Committee noting t he various initiatives being taken under the scheme of 
Pharmacovigilance initiatives, observes that the Ministry is in the process of building a 
network/structure for carrying out strict monitoring/vigilance of quality control of 
ASU&H drugs.  The Committe e feels that this 3 -tier network of pharmacovigilance 
needs to play pro-active role in reporting adverse drug events along with surveillance of 
misleading advertisements. With the Steering & Monitoring Committee, Technical 
Advisory Committee and Central Si gnal Detection & Causality Assessment Committee 
have been set up to assist in efficient implementation action of the said scheme , t he 
Committee hopes that the task relating to the well-being of patients consuming ASU&H 
drugs will be taken care of . The Committee emphasizes upon the need for imparting 
training and capacity building and also the awareness generation of ASU&H 
Pharmacovigilance so as to educate all involved in the network of pharmacovigilance  
for successful implementation of the scheme.   
(Para 5.5) 
 

30 
 
NATIONAL AYUSH MISSION (NAM) 
 The Committee finds that financial performance during 2014-15 indicates a huge 
gap between the amount approved by EFC/Cabinet and the actual allocation of funds 
for NAM.  The Committee is, however, pleased to note full utilization of allocated funds 
for NAM during the years 2014 -15 to 2017-18.  This also indicates  potential absorption 
capacity of funds under various components within the scheme. The Committee 
understands that the scheme is vital as it encompas ses not just upgradation of AYUSH 
hospitals and dispensaries, but also that of AYUSH educational institutions, drug 
testing laboratories. Moreover, the scheme aims to produce quality medicinal plants 
including adequate supply for AYUSH/herbal industry. The  Committee, therefore, 
recommends that funds earmarked for the scheme must be released for accomplishment 
of the major objectives of the scheme.   
(Para 6.4) 
 The Committee finds that there are several components under NAM which are 
of immense importance. The quarter -wise activities to be completed in 2020 -21 show 
that adequate funds will be required for upgradation of AYUSH hospitals and 
dispensaries, AYUSH units co -located in health facilities for 50 bedded integrated 
AYUSH hospitals, AYUSH educational in stitutions, States drug testing labs, drug 
testing lab samples, functional State/PSU Pharmacies and AYUSH Health & Wellness 
Centers. The Committee understands that these outreach activities under NAM aim to 
streamline the AYUSH public health delivery syste m, its educational system and also 
streamline the standardization and quality control of ASU&H drugs through its 
support to drug testing labs. The Committee believes that these components if 
effectively implemented and monitored would go a long way in increasing the credibility 
of AYUSH systems and present them as a viable alternative to the modern system of 
medicine. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends the Ministry to ensure the 
achievement of physical as well as financial targets of the scheme through strict 
monitoring the execution of the scheme without time and cost overruns.  The Committee 
would also like to reiterate that the funds allocated should be used judiciously as well as 
optimally.  
(Para 6.8) 
RESEARCH COUNCILS 
 The Committee observes that in the year 2018 -19, against the projected demand 
of Rs. 997.90 crore, Rs. 608.97 crore was allocated at the RE stage of which Rs. 582.27 
crore were utilized   amounting to almost 95.6% of the RE allocation. However, the 
Committee is constrained to o bserve that the amount allocated to each Research 
Council is   much lower as compared to the projected demand. The Committee further 
finds that in the year 2019 -20, Rs. 672.32 crore has been allocated at RE stage against 
the projected demand of Rs 1024.86 crore. A sum of Rs. 568.04 crore has been utilized 
till 10.02.2020 which comes to approximately 84.45 % of total allocation at RE stage. 
The Committee appreciates the potential absorption capacity of these Research 
Councils. 
(Para 7.5) 
 The Committee finds that trend of utilization in last two financial years is good 
and hopes that remaining 16% of budget will be utilized by the Ministry before the 
conclusion of the current financial year. The Committee is, however, unhappy to note 
that despite the good trend in utilization of funds, the allocation of budget at BE stage in 

31 
 
the year 2020-21 is less than the budget allocated at RE 2019 -20. The Committee fails to 
comprehend the reason for reduction in the budget. The Committee is of the view that  
the Ministry of Finance should consider the potential absorption capacity of these 
Research Councils and the set physical  targets in the Output and Outcome Statement 
while allocating the funds for intended purpose. 
(Para 7.6) 
 The Committee is angui shed to note such a low allocation of budget to the 
Research Councils as compared to their projected demand. Which Government   is 
attempting to mainstream AYUSH systems of medicine on the one hand, such a low 
allocation to Research Councils on the other w ill not only restrict the research activities 
in these councils but would further hinder the development of AYUSH services within 
the country.  The Committee is of the view that Research is an ongoing activity and is a 
long drawn process requiring adequate  funds. These Research Councils certainly need 
adequate budgetary support for continuing their researches and also to promote more 
and more research activities/projects . The Committee would also like to highlight that 
tangible outcomes of these researches would  incentivize the students at large willing to 
opt for Indian system of medicine. Keeping this in mind, the Committee is of the firm 
view that the allocation of budget to these Councils should be enhanced.  The 
Committee, accordingly, recommends the M inistry to persuade Ministry of Finance for 
the higher allocation of Budgetary provision  at the RE stage. 
(Para 7.7) 
 The Committee notes that the CCRUM, CCRYN, CCRH and CCRS are in the 
process of applying/obtaining accreditation from the National Accredi tation Board for 
Hospitals and healthcare providers (NABH). The Committee has been emphasizing 
upon the adherence to the minimal required parameters and other quality indicators 
which are essential for improving quality of research in particular and qualit y of 
healthcare service in general. The Committee recommends that all the Research 
Councils/Institutes must obtain NABH accreditation without much procrastination. 
(Para 7.9) 
NORTH EASTERN AREAS 
 The Committee has been consistently emphasizing on the need for increasing 
the budgetary outlay of different Institutes and Schemes under AYUSH. However, the 
Committee is dismayed to note that some of the apex AYUSH institutes which are 
envisaged for mainstreaming of AYUSH services have fared poorly in the optimum 
utilisation of its budget. The Committee notes that though the budget allocated to 
various Institutes and Schemes under the NER in FY 2018 -19 & 2019 -20 is quite low, 
the actual expenditure under these Schemes and Institutes is still below the allocated 
budget.  
(Para 8.7) 
 The Committee also observes that the budget outlay of NEIFM, which was 
established to create an interface between traditional/folk medicine practitioners and 
research in the field, has over the years reduced drastic ally. Expenditure of Rs. 0.78 
crore in 2018-19 and Rs. 0.92 crore speaks volume of the neglected state of the Institute. 
The Committee also takes note of the submission of the Ministry that the Institute has 
seen an upward trend in the inflow of the patien ts. The Committee observes that the 

32 
 
Institute has failed to fill all the sanctioned scientific posts. The Committee, therefore, 
strongly, recommends the Ministry to ensure that appointment process of all the 
sanctioned posts are completed in a time frame a nd the Institute is able to effectively 
utilise the allocated budget.  
(Para 8.8) 
 
 The Committee also notes that there has been an increase in the budget 
allocation under NAM (HWC) {Rs.17.00 crores} and NAM (GBS) [Rs.54.00 crores] in 
BE 2020-2021. The Committee strongly recommends that the Budget allocated must be 
optimally utilised and the envisioned aim of co -location of AYUSH facilities at 
PHCs/CHCs/DHs under NAM must be fulfilled. 
(Para 8.9) 
 The Committee believes that North East India has the potenti al to strengthen 
the AYUSH system in the country. Considering its rich biodiversity , the Committee 
calls upon the Ministry to make concerted efforts to explore the rich resource of 
medicinal plants in the region. The Committee also believes that the servic es of the 
AYUSH practitioners can be successfully utilised in improving the delivery of quality 
healthcare services in the North East. The Committee believes that AYUSH can emerge 
as a reliable healthcare treatment and provide an alternative medicine syste m to a 
region that is poorly connected with the mainland India.  
(Para 8.10)

PREFACE 
I, the Chairman of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health 
and Family Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its 
behalf, present this One Hundred Twenty First  Report of the Committee on Action Taken by 
Government on the Recommendations/ Observations contained in One Hundred Tenth Report on 
Functioning of Food Safety and Standards Authority of India.  
2. The One Hundred Tenth Report of the Department -related Par liamentary Standing 
Committee on Health and Family Welfare was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of 
Lok Sabha on 9 th August, 2018. Action Taken Note of the Government on the recommendations 
contained in the Report was received from the Ministr y on 4th February, 2019 .  Two sets of

CHAPTER–I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1 It has been given to understand that FSSAI is presently operating with staff from 
state apparatus.  The Committee opines that FSSAI cannot function to its optimum level 
without employing technical persons as permanent staff.  The Committee recommends that 
FSSAI should be restructured and persons with domain knowledge and expertise in the food 
sector should be employed to run organization.  
 
1.2 The Committee notes the shortcomings pointed out in CAG report about the 
administration of food safety laws.  The Committee opines that there is a need to restructure 
or revamp the FSSAI so as to enable it to meet the multiple challenges in the arena of food 
safety and regulation. The Committee, therefore, recommends that only technically 
competent officers with exper tise in subject of food science should be appointed/ selected in 
FSSAI so that they are most suitable for the task assigned to them by FSS Act 2006. 
(Para 1.20 & 1.53) 
Action Taken 
 
1.3 The Ministry submitted that the Recruitment Regulations notified on 1s t October 
2018 and the posts sanctioned at various levels by Government are based on the 
organizational restructuring of FSSAI.  The mandate of FSSAI under the Food Safety and 
Standards Act, 2006 is to ensure safe and wholesome food for human consumption. This 
overarching mandate calls for action on traditional regulatory functions (setting standards, 
regulations, enforcement, food testing, risk management, research etc.), combined with the 
need for capacity building and consumer empowerment.  Accordingly, the Recruitment 
Regulations have 3 broad categories of posts to fulfill the mandate viz. Scientific and 
Technical posts (that constitute the bulk of the posts): IT and Specialized Services (including 
inter-alia training and capacity building, social and be havioural change communication etc.) 
and Support Services. Hence, the structure of the organization has been carefully created to 
ensure that the varied nature of its functions are handled effectively. 
 
1.4 The Ministry also submitted the following details: 
 
 135 posts have been re -designated at various levels as per details at Annexure 1.This 
re-designation reflects the enhanced job description in the light of evolving functions 
of the Authority, and also the merging of numerous fragmented cadres and sub -cadres 
into 3 major groups as brought out above, for smoother administration and better 
career growth prospects. 
 Of the 824 posts sanctioned, 415 posts have been advertised at various levels in the 
first phase of recruitment. Almost 1.6 lakhs applications ha ve been received against 
the advertised posts and a robust selection procedure, comprising of a Computer 
Based Test, Written Examination and Interview (as applicable) is in place. The exams 
are scheduled in July 2019 and September/October 2019.  The second  phase of 
recruitment will be taken up after the completion of the first phase, with the aim to 
complete the recruitment process within a period of 2 years.  
 The contractual employees have been given weightage  in selection and have an 
opportunity to appear and qualify through the selection process. Further, since the 

2 
 
process of recruitment is being taken up in phases, contractual employees would have 
more than 1 opportunity to prepare and participate in the selection process 
 
1.5 The Ministry further submitted that the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India 
(FSSAI) has advertised a total 307 vacancies at various levels in Phase -I of recruitment 
process vide Advt. No. DR-01/2019, DR-02/2019 & DR-03/2019. 
  
1.6 The recruitment process for 04 posts of Director and 06 posts of Food Analyst 
advertised against Advt. No. Dr-01/2019 and DR-03/2019 has been completed. Against these 
posts,  of the selected persons, 3 are contractual employees of FSSAI.   Selection pr ocess for 
other posts is going on and is likely to be completed by end of this year. Second phase of 
recruitment will be started thereafter. All vacant posts will be included in the second phase of 
recruitment. 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.7 The Committee notes that as per the information available on the website of FSSAI, 
out of its 9 members of Central Advisory Committee (CAC) representing the interests of food 
industry, agriculture, consumers relevant research bodies and food laboratories, 5 are from 
Delhi.  The ex -officio Chairman of CAC is also Delhi based which makes this number six.  
Given the fact that there are 24 chapters under trade laws dealing with food and scope of 
FSSAI and there is vast pool of expertise available country -wide, this Delhi cen tric 
composition of CAC hardly represent various interest groups.  The Committee feels that this 
factor is certainly depriving FSSAI of the sage advice and expertise of the immense talent 
present in the food sector in the country.  This also leads the Committee to the conclusion that 
there is no transparent procedure for selection of members of CAC.   
1.8 The Committee, therefore, recommends that there should be written guidelines on the 
selection process of members of CAC and the whole selection criteria s hould be made 
transparent.  Bio data of selected candidates and their areas on competency/proven track 
record should be displayed on the website of FSSAI.  It also recommends that the 
composition of CAC be broad based so that the pool of expertise in the f ood sector spread 
across the country could be tapped. 
(Para 1.25 & 1.26) 
Action Taken 
1.9 The recommendations of the Committee have been accepted and a transparent 
procedure for selection of members of CAC has been initiated. 
Recommendation /Observation 
 
1.10 The Committee observes that the responsibility for surveillance and enforcement of 
food laws lies squarely on the State/UT Governments.  But given the resource crunch in the 
States, it would be unrealistic to expect that the States would be in a positi on to improve the 
infrastructure and increase the manpower without central assistance for overhauling their 
food regulatory system. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Health 
and Family Welfare should work out a fully Centrally Sponso red Scheme for up-gradation of 
manpower, strengthening of food safety infrastructure including food testing laboratories and 
setting up a robust surveillance system at State level.  
(Para 1.42)
